Multimorbidity and
long-term conditions

What happens when one person has several conditions, but care is organised one condition at a time?

Three ideas today: care organised one condition at a time creates work, and the work lands on the person · how common this is depends on what we count, and a population figure plans a service, not a Tuesday · deprivation brings complexity forward, into working life.

Contemporary Issues | Week 3The claim
Open · before anything else · 4 minutes

“The evidence shows this pathway works.”

Imagine tomorrow your manager, your tutor, or a colleague says that to you. Before you repeat it to somebody else, what would you want to know?

What would you want to know? Say it as a question you would actually ask.
Every question you ask is about one of four things: the source · what it can support · what it cannot establish · what you would still need to know.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Three weeks in
Three weeks in · 4 minutes

What is this module helping you practise?

Different starting points are expected. You do not need the same experience to take part.

At Level 9, knowledge is the starting point. The work is interpreting evidence, recognising limits and making a defensible judgement.

The tools are here to help you practise that. Today: the Evidence Log.

You do not need to start from the same place. You do need to arrive at the same kind of judgement.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The Evidence Log
The Evidence Log · the one on Brightspace since Week 1

Your questions are the four judgement questions at the heart of the Evidence Log

WeekIssue or caseSource (Cite Them Right Harvard)One claim it supportsOne thing it cannot tell meMy next question
contextcontextWhat is the source?What exactly can it support?What can it not establish?What do I still need?

The first two columns are just where you are in the module. The four on the right are a routine for handling every question you just asked.

That is what the Evidence Log is for. It is not a list of things you have read. One row a week, from Week 1 to Week 8. You have one row already, from the stations.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Build one row
Worked example · one source you met last week · build it live

Wyper et al. (2023): minimum unit pricing in Scotland

What the study did, in plain words. Compared deaths and hospital admissions from alcohol in Scotland with England, before and after Scotland put a floor under the price of alcohol in May 2018. Thirty-two months of data. Published in The Lancet.

Source, in Harvard

Wyper, G.M.A. et al. (2023) ‘Evaluating the impact of alcohol minimum unit pricing on deaths and hospitalisations in Scotland: a controlled interrupted time series study’, The Lancet, 401(10385), pp. 1361–1370.

One claim it supports

After the price floor, alcohol deaths in Scotland were lower than expected, with the largest fall in the most deprived areas.

One thing it cannot tell me

It strengthens the case for an effect (a controlled design, England as comparison) but cannot rule out every other explanation. Follow-up was 32 months. The hospitalisation result was uncertain. And the 50p price it evaluated no longer exists.

My next question

Has anything changed since the price rose to 65p in 2024? And what did it do to people who drink heavily but are not in the poorest areas?
One row, four cells, built together. Notice how much of the paper you have to read to fill the third cell. That is the work.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Recorded or interrogated
The difference the log makes

Recording a source is not the same as interrogating it

Recorded

“Wyper 2023. MUP works.”

A note. True as far as it goes. You cannot defend it, because you cannot say what it rests on or where it stops.

Interrogated

The row you just built

Source. What it supports. What it cannot establish. What you would need next. A judgement you can defend, in a meeting or an essay.

One question to ask of every row, out loud, not as a column: what could this evidence inform in practice or in how a service is designed? For MUP: pricing policy, yes. What to say to one person about their drinking, no.
The promise is not “your reference list writes itself”. It is this: by Unit 8 you will have a bank of evidence you have already interrogated, not fifteen PDFs you vaguely remember reading.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Meet Mr H
Now the subject · 5 minutes

Meet Mr H

Fictional case for teaching

Mr H, 58

Type 2 diabetes, COPD, depression. Several medicines. Lives alone in a damp flat. Redundant four months ago; waiting on benefits; some weeks short of food. No car: the health centre is two buses, 90 minutes each way. Discharged three weeks ago after a COPD flare-up.

Teaching vignette · imagined voice

“Everybody I see is nice. Everybody gives me something to do. The diabetes nurse wants me walking. The chest people want me at a class twice a week across town. The mental health lady wants a diary. I get letters. I get texts. Some weeks I don't open them. I'm not lazy. I'm just done by Wednesday.”

One word each: what did his profile make you assume? We will come back to your words later.
Three questions carry today: What is he being asked to do? Is he unusual? Each condition has good guidance, so where is the problem?
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Two words
Two words, plainly · before anything else is built on them

Long-term condition. Multimorbidity.

Long-term condition

A health condition that lasts, usually a year or more, and affects a person's life. It can be managed; it is not usually cured. Diabetes. COPD. Depression. Each of Mr H's three is one.

About half of Scottish adults report at least one. Fewer live with several.

Multimorbidity

One person living with two or more long-term conditions at the same time. Mr H has three. The word matters because care is usually organised one condition at a time, and he is not one condition.

How common that is depends on what you count. Block 2 will show you why.

One line, then move on: noncommunicable disease overlaps with long-term condition but is not the same thing. LTCs also include mental health conditions, HIV managed long term, and post-COVID condition.
If you have met these words before, good. If not, that is all they mean. Everything today is built from them.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Block 1
Block 1 · 0:20 – 0:55

What is he being asked to do?

Before any term, before any number. Two ordinary documents, and the work hidden inside them.

Every question in this block has two routes. Route one: from Mr H, for everyone. Route two, optional: from work or placement, if you have it. No names.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The letter
Artefact one · a clinic letter · what work is hidden in this?

Read it as Mr H would

Fictional teaching artefact — not an NHS document

Respiratory Service · [Health board]
Ref RESP/H/2260913

Dear Mr H,

Following your recent admission, you have been referred to the Pulmonary Rehabilitation Programme. Your assessment appointment is:

Tuesday 13 October, 14:10
Physiotherapy Department, Level 2, [Hospital name], [Address]

Please arrive 15 minutes early and bring a list of your current medicines, your inhalers, and comfortable clothing and shoes. If accepted onto the programme, classes run twice weekly for six weeks at the same location.

If you cannot attend, please telephone 0141 000 0000 (Mon–Fri, 9–4) to rearrange. Failure to attend without notice may result in discharge from the service.

Route one · everyone

What does Mr H have to do for this letter to work? Not what it says. What it asks of him.

Read every line, including the last one.

Route two · optional

If you have seen a letter like this land on someone, what did they do with it?

Nobody wrote a bad letter. A correct letter still transfers work to the person who receives it.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The list
Artefact two · a repeat medicines list · what has to happen for this to be taken as written?

Seven items. Three conditions. One person.

Fictional teaching artefact — not a real prescription

MedicineWhenNote
Metformin 500mgTwice daily, with food
Gliclazide 80mgMorning, with breakfastDose changed 2 weeks ago
Tiotropium inhalerOnce daily
Salbutamol inhalerAs required
Fostair inhalerTwice daily; rinse mouth after
Sertraline 100mgMorning
Atorvastatin 20mgNightReview due

Route one · everyone

Pick one line. What has to happen, every day, for it to be taken as written? Then: what happens when the pharmacy is a bus away, one item changed, one is running out, and “with food” on a week he is short of food?

Route two · optional

Where might a service you know unintentionally create work for the person it supports?

Every item is clinically sensible. The list is right. Living the list is the work.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Name it
Now the word for what you just found

What does Mr H actually have to do because he has these conditions?

You have just listed it from two documents. Appointments. Medicines. Blood tests. Monitoring. An exercise programme. Phone calls. Forms. Travel. Remembering. Making different services fit together.

Researchers call this treatment burden: the work of being a patient. The illness creates work. Care can create more. You found the work first; now it has a name.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Three burdens
Three kinds of burden · a module teaching tool, not a framework to cite

Separate them before you judge

Condition burden

What the illnesses themselves do: symptoms, pain, breathlessness, low mood, limitation.

Treatment burden

The work of managing them: medicines, appointments, tests, monitoring, exercises.

System burden

Extra work when care does not join up: repeated journeys, duplication, conflicting advice, coordination and gaps.

Route one: which of the three does the medicines list create? Which does the letter create? Route two, optional: could a service be clinically correct and still create unreasonable burden?
These are teaching categories, not three perfectly separate boxes. Some things overlap. That is where your judgement comes in.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Three pathways
Each pathway is reasonable on its own · three professional lenses

Every pathway makes sense on its own

Diabetes sees

Bloods / HbA1c · retinal screening · foot check · medicines · diet and activity advice. It sees blood sugar and feet.

Respiratory sees

Inhaler review · pulmonary rehabilitation · vaccinations · exacerbation action plan · follow-up. It sees breathlessness.

Mental health sees

Therapy · medicines · mood or activity plan · follow-up · everyday routine. It sees mood, and “engagement”.

Route one: is anything here unreasonable? Now put all three around one person. Mr H sees the whole month. Who else does? Route two, optional: in a setting you know, who would hold the whole picture, if anyone?
Individually reasonable does not mean collectively manageable. Three good lenses, and none of them sees the month.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The mismatch
One person, three guidelines · the quotation is Barnett et al. (2012)

“Health systems are largely configured for individual diseases rather than multimorbidity”

NICE NG56 adds the precise point: the evidence behind single-condition guidelines often comes from people without multimorbidity, and it asks clinicians to consider treatment burden, interactions and what matters to the person. Scotland's 2026 polypharmacy guidance opens its review with “what matters to the individual?” Hold that; it is next week's first question.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Workload and capacity
Simple teaching lens · make the imbalance visible

What happens when the workload of care exceeds the person's capacity?

Workload

What care asks Mr H to carry

Appointments · medicines · tests and monitoring · travel · forms · exercise and lifestyle changes · coordinating services.

Capacity

What he has available to carry it

Time · money · energy · physical and mental health · transport · support · understanding · competing life demands.

Route one: what has Mr H got to carry this with? Route two, optional: what might you need to ask that a disease-specific assessment would miss?
When workload is greater than capacity, something is delayed, missed or dropped. This is a lens for thinking about burden, not a score for judging the person.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The record line
Challenge the first explanation · a documentation exercise

Six weeks later, this is in his notes

Respiratory · contact note · 24/11

Did not attend pulmonary rehabilitation. Not engaging with treatment.

First reaction

What is yours? A reaction is not yet a judgement.

What do we know?

He did not attend. That is all this line establishes.

What don't we know?

Why. The buses. The Tuesday. The letter he did not open. The breathlessness that makes the walk to the bus stop the hardest part of the day.

Route one: why might someone miss four appointments? Everyone can answer from Mr H. Route two, optional: those working in services, what explanations do records sometimes give?
Carry forward the Week 2 habit: what a person does is not an explanation on its own. This line converts one observation into a verdict on a person.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The rewrite
Two minutes · on paper · everyone

Rewrite it. One or two lines. What would you put in the record instead?

02:00

The test for your line

Does it separate what was observed from what was assumed? Does it say what you do not know? Would the next professional who reads it know what to do?

One version, after you have written yours

“Did not attend PR assessment 13/10. Reason not yet established. Previous notes record no car, two-bus journey, recent redundancy and low mood. Contact Mr H to establish reason and discuss any support needed before re-referral.”
When you compare: what did you keep, what did you take out, and what did you add that was not there? Route two, optional: what can the original line do downstream, once it is in a record?
Same patient. Different sentence. Different care. Many of you will write or rely on records like this; others will inherit their consequences.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Beyond the clinic
The burden does not stop at the clinic

Where does the work land?

Person

Symptoms · time · medicines · travel · money · remembering. Mr H, mostly, because he lives alone.

Family and unpaid support

Caring · time · work · coordination. When there is somebody, a large share of the treatment and coordination work moves onto them, usually unasked. Unit 5 takes this properly.

Services and society

Staff time · service use · employment · participation. The consequences travel beyond health care: being “done by Wednesday” can make looking for, or returning to, work harder.

Route one: who carries Mr H's coordination work right now? Route two, optional: in a setting you know, who ends up doing it?
Population figures for unpaid care and for the cost of ill health are in the Sway, with their limits. In the room, the point is simpler: the work has to land somewhere, and the system rarely asks where.

Contemporary Issues | Week 3Block 2
Block 2 · 1:05 – 1:40

Is he unusual, and what is that evidence for?

Now the numbers have a job. You have seen what one person's month looks like. How many people is that? Why him at 58? And what can a population figure tell a service that it cannot tell a practitioner?

Two numbers today, and each one teaches an idea. Everything else with a percentage on it is in the Sway, with its source and its limit attached.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Prevalence
One word, plainly · before the counter

What prevalence is, and why estimates differ

Prevalence

Out of everyone in a population, how many have the thing right now. Usually a percentage. “23% of adults are multimorbid” means: count the adults, count the ones with two or more conditions, divide.

Why two studies disagree

Because they made different choices before counting. Which conditions are on the list? Two or more, or three or more? Whose records: GP, hospital, a survey? What age range? Which country, which year? Change one choice and the number moves.

Route one: if you counted only diabetes and COPD, is Mr H multimorbid? If you counted only heart disease and cancer? Route two, optional: where have you seen a figure quoted without the definition behind it?
So a prevalence figure is never just a number. It is a number plus a list plus a method. Watch that happen on the next slide.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The counter
Watch it move · the counter on screen

How many are multimorbid if we count two conditions? Eighty?

One study. Same 1,168,260 people every time. The only thing that changes is how many conditions the researchers decided to count.

Counting the two commonest

4.6%. MacRae et al. (2023), 1.17 million people.

Counting ten

29.5%. The number moves fastest early.

Counting all eighty

40.5%. Plateaus from about 52. Nine published lists: 11.1% to 36.4%.
Researchers call this heterogeneity. You have just seen it. A figure counts what it counts: attach the definition. So: Mr H is not unusual.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Two jobs
The distinction that makes the numbers useful · and the Component 2 rubric, taught as a way of thinking

Population evidence and individual care do different jobs

Population evidence asks

How common? Who is affected? Where are the patterns? What might services need to plan for: workforce, caseload, pathway design, coordination capacity, where to put resources?

Individual care asks

What is happening for this person? What matters to them? What capacity and support do they have? What response is appropriate here, now?

Route one: which column does the counter belong in? Which column does the record line belong in? Route two, optional: when has a population figure been used, in a place you know, to decide something about one person?
Prevalence can help plan a service. It cannot tell us what Mr H needs on Tuesday. Your assessment asks for both levels. So does health and social care practice, and service planning.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3The chain, recalled
Ninety seconds · you built this last week

Why is Mr H ill? You already know how to answer that.

Box 1

Circumstances

Redundant. Benefits pending. Damp flat. No car.

Box 2

What he's next to

A damp flat. Two buses to the health centre. Whatever is near a flat like that.

Box 3

Stress and resources

Waiting on benefits, some weeks short of food. Lives alone. Low mood. Little control over his day.

Box 4

Built up over a life

These circumstances can accumulate over time and shape risk. Barnett lets us test whether that pattern appears at population level.

Last week's question was why is she ill? This week's is different: why is he ill at 58, and not at 75? Box four is the answer, and the next slide puts a number on it.
If you missed Week 2: this is the five-box chain. What a person does is box five. Four boxes come before it.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Earlier, how much?
Before the number · one prediction

He is 58. Would you expect complexity in more deprived communities to appear a little earlier, or substantially earlier?

A little earlier

A couple of years. Deprivation nudges it.

Substantially earlier

A decade or more. Deprivation moves it into a different stage of life.

Pick one, and say why. The point is not the guess; it is whether the answer changes how you picture a 58-year-old in a poorer area.
Same health service. Same country. Same free GP. The gap between your expectation and the evidence is where the learning is. Neither scenario on the next slides describes any real service.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Earlier
Barnett et al. (2012) · 1,751,841 people · 314 Scottish practices

Recorded multimorbidity occurred 10 to 15 years earlier

Contemporary Issues | Week 3Same age, different risk
Unpack · what ten to fifteen years actually means

Same age. Different population risk.

Mr H

58. Three conditions: diabetes, COPD, depression. Several medicines. Two buses to the health centre. Redundant; waiting on a benefits decision. We have not said which decile he lives in; we do not need to.

His month is the one you will map this afternoon.

A man in the least deprived tenth

58. In Barnett's Scottish data, comparable levels of recorded multimorbidity appeared in the least deprived areas roughly 10 to 15 years later than in the most deprived.

A population difference, not a forecast about this man: it says when complexity typically arrives, not what will happen to him.

What can ten or fifteen earlier years of complexity mean for somebody’s working life, income, caring responsibilities and family life?
Populations, not predictions. And a ten to fifteen year difference in when complexity arrives is a difference in a working life.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Age and deprivation
Two drivers

Age matters. But deprivation brings complexity forward.

Age

Multimorbidity becomes more common as populations get older. Across a large pooled review, prevalence was higher in studies with older participants. And in Barnett’s Scottish data, more of the people with several conditions were under 65 than over, because there are more of them.

Deprivation

In Barnett's Scottish study, multimorbidity occurred 10 to 15 years earlier in the most deprived areas. Same mechanism as Week 2, a new outcome: disadvantage changes when complexity arrives.

Two minutes with a neighbour: if your first thought about Mr H was smoking or diet, what produced them? Those are the last link. Individual behaviour is not an explanation by itself.
02:00
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Mind and body
Physical and mental together · an interaction, not a third box

Does Mr H experience three neat categories because the system records three?

Depression changes the work

Low mood makes the diary, the inhaler routine, the bus and the class harder to start. The treatment for the other two conditions gets heavier.

Breathlessness changes the life

COPD limits walking, going out, seeing people. Less activity, less contact, less control. That is where the mood goes.

And it comes back round

Worse mood, less self-management, worse sugars and breathing, worse mood. Three records. One month.

Route one: which of his three conditions makes the other two harder to manage? Route two, optional: which service, in a setting you know, would notice that?
Barnett found mental and physical conditions together were nearly twice as common in the most deprived areas. Mr H's depression is not a separate story from his lungs. It is the same month.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Different arrangements
International transfer · three minutes · a device you know from Week 1

Same Mr H. Different arrangements. What changes, and what does not?

03:00
Teaching scenario A · assume

Formal services exist, free at the point of use, organised separately

Assume: diabetes, respiratory and mental health each have their own clinic, records and appointment system. None routinely sees the others' notes. Nobody is paid to see the month.

Teaching scenario B · assume

Formal services are few; more is paid for out of pocket; coordination falls to family

Assume: one clinic, when he can afford it. Medicines bought when there is money. A sister or a neighbour does the remembering, the fetching, the deciding when to go.

Route one: who coordinates in A? In B? Who carries the treatment work in each? Route two, optional: where you know, who would this fall to?
The arrangements differ. The coordination problem may not. Multimorbidity is not a rich-country problem; the figures are in the Sway. The question travels: how much work, who coordinates, what happens when services work separately, what resources, what assumptions.

Contemporary Issues | Week 3Four questions
Lecturer synthesis · connect the evidence

Four questions on multimorbidity

QuestionOne line, from this week
1 ProblemHalf of adults report a condition; fewer have several; in deprived areas it arrives 10 to 15 years earlier. Population evidence plans the service. It cannot tell you what Mr H needs on Tuesday.
5 EvidenceHow common is it? Depends on what you count: the counter moved from 4.6% to 40.5% on one dataset. Attach the definition.
3 SystemConfigured for individual diseases; three good lenses and none sees the month; care can add work to illness.
8 PracticeSee the month, not the condition. Notice what nobody coordinates. Do not stop at behaviour. Write the record line you would defend.
2, 4, 6, 7Determinants, policy, equity, context: met this week, developed in Units 2 and 4.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Judgement
Lecturer synthesis · judgement · about 7 minutes

Condition, treatment, system

Condition burden

What the illnesses themselves do.

Treatment burden

The work of managing them. Necessary care can still create work.

System burden

Work produced or intensified because care does not join up.

One judgement per group: which burden in Mr H's month is most preventable or most intensified by the organisation of care? Give one source, one limit, and one thing a service could stop expecting him to coordinate himself. Some read aloud. Part C asks for your own.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3One row, now
Five minutes · on paper · the Week 3 row, done in the room

One source from today. Claim. Limitation. Next question.

05:00

MacRae et al. (2023)

The counter. What it supports; what it cannot say about any one person.

Barnett et al. (2012)

10 to 15 years. Population, not prediction. 2012 data.

NICE NG56

The evidence behind single-condition guidance may not represent people with multimorbidity. Limit: guidance says what should be considered, not whether it happens.

Scottish Government (2026)

Polypharmacy: “what matters to the individual?” Intention, not evidence of practice.

Then, out loud: what will you notice differently after today, on your next shift, placement, or the next time you are near a service? One sentence. That is the point of the module.

Contemporary Issues | Week 3Hand-off
Final 3 minutes · carry one question into Unit 4

Mr H's month is broken. How should health and social care respond without simply giving him more work to coordinate?

Next week

We test possible responses: shared decision-making, self-management support, self-directed support, co-production and integrated care. Mr H comes back; this time you design. And you will judge each response by one question: does it reduce the work, or move it?

Before Unit 4

Part C: your judgement. Your row into the Evidence Log. Open the Unit 4 pre-read in the Sway; it is short. Keep today's sheet: your diagnosis is the brief.

“What matters to the individual?” Hold that phrase. It is next week's first question.
Contemporary Issues | Week 3Key takeaways
Close · three sentences to remember

What Week 3 leaves you with

1

Population evidence and individual care do different jobs. Prevalence plans a service; it cannot tell you what one person needs on Tuesday. And how common depends on what you count: attach the definition.

2

Deprivation brings complexity forward, by 10 to 15 years in Barnett's Scottish study, into working life. Mind and body do not sit in separate boxes; they make each other's work harder.

3

Three sensible pathways can create one very difficult life. Condition, treatment, system: separate them before you judge. And never let one missed appointment become a verdict on a person.

Sources: Barnett et al. (2012) · MacRae et al. (2023) · NICE NG56 · Scottish Government (2026) · Wyper et al. (2023). Full references, the moved figures and the Evidence Log guidance are in the Sway and the activity sheet.
